The Invisible Man Authorship. Two major novels titled The Invisible Man or Invisible Man exist by different authors in different centuries, and they are often confused or conflated. H.G. Wells wrote The Invisible Man in 1897 as a science-fiction parable about a scientist who discovers invisibility. Ralph Ellison wrote Invisible Man in 1952 as a philosophical novel about race and identity in America. Beyond the title, they share virtually nothing in premise, theme, or era.

Wells's Invisible Man concerns a scientist named Griffin who makes himself invisible through scientific experimentation and descends into madness and violence. It is science fiction and social critique. Ellison's Invisible Man follows an unnamed Black protagonist through American society, exploring racism and the erasure of Black identity. The invisibility here is metaphorical and existential, not literal.

Wells's novel is brief and action-driven, exploring what happens when a man seizes ultimate power through invisibility. Ellison's is a sprawling 600-page introspection on American racism. Wells wrote his story during the late Victorian era and was influenced by emerging scientific romance. Ellison wrote after World War II and drew from modernist literature and African-American tradition.

The titles are often confused in educational and cultural contexts, leading to mistaken expectations or misidentification of which work is being referenced. Both novels are considered classics, but for entirely different reasons. Wells pioneered science-fiction concepts with his story, while Ellison made a landmark contribution to American literature and racial discourse.
